synopsis: The braking system must work across machine models with different sizes and sensor positions, but mounting-dependent blind areas prevent evidence from transferring freely; the existing proximity-awareness system took years of calibration to balance detection and false positives [f286, f11552, f10]. Physics-based sensor models can respond causally to changed sensor pose, but no published perception-evidence transfer approach or universally acceptable off-road transfer distance or angle was found; new mounting heights should be expected to require retraining or adaptation, not just threshold changes [f4466, f370, f7905, f7037]. Raw-log replay is limited to recorded sensors, mounts and scenarios, and raw detections and per-sensor statistics are not comparable when modality, mounting or processing changes [f5166, f5211]. Mounting geometry has demonstrated practical consequences: NIOSH found that one rear radar missed people near haul-truck rear tyres, while two antennas approximately 1.8 m apart with beams crossed inward approximately 20 degrees improved detection there [f7039, f7040]. Planning should retain physical characterization at mounting-geometry extremes, document calibration and measurement uncertainty, and validate each sensor technology and mounting family against withheld real raw data; a sensor change in 2027 would invalidate multiple evidence streams, and a validated sensor digital twin should not be claimed before hardware and mounting are frozen and correlated [f7885, f9729, f10558, f11912, f11917].
